Proof-Carrying Regulatory and Jurisdictional Compliance, Authority Graphs, Versioned Codes and Standards, Incorporation by Reference, Applicability, Exceptions, Waivers and Variances, Alternative Means and Methods, Permit and Inspection State Machines, Appeals, Professional Responsibility, and Jurisdiction-Specific Release
Legal-Scope and Source Convention
This paper develops mathematical and formal regulatory semantics. It does not provide individualized legal advice and does not claim that its formal structures constitute actual law, legal interpretation, or legal enforceability.
No contemporary real-world code edition, statute, permit procedure, jurisdictional adoption, or regulatory interpretation is used as a substantive premise. Every regulatory rule, edition, amendment, authority, date, permit process, and numerical threshold appearing in a worked example is explicitly synthetic.
The permanent boundary is:
[ \boxed{ \text{formal regulatory model} \neq \text{authoritative legal interpretation}. } ]



Abstract

When the governing authority state is unresolved, ANANKE preserves a nonempty family:

It then distinguishes:
\bigcap_{L\in\mathfrak L_{J_t}} \mathcal A_{\mathrm{reg}}(L) } ]

\left{ \pi: \pi \text{ is an admissible regulatory process reaching the declared release state under modality }\mu \right}. } ]

The governing doctrine is:
[ \boxed{ \begin{minipage}{0.91\linewidth} A building is not regulatorily certified merely because an engineering model says it is safe or because a rule checker found no violation. Regulatory status exists only relative to the correct jurisdiction, effective authority sources, adoption history, applicability predicates, amendments, exceptions, approved deviations, permit state, inspection scope, evidence, and authority decisions. \end{minipage} } ]



1. Prompt-20 Body Audit
The complete Prompt-20 body was audited rather than treating its permanent registry as proof.
￼
Audit conclusion
The Prompt-20 body contains the load-bearing definitions and proofs required by Prompt 21.
No registry-only theorem is imported.
No Prompt-20 Completion Addendum is required.
Permanent inherited limitations include:
A formal contract transition is not a permit transition.
Contract permission does not create regulatory authority.
Strategic implementation does not prove regulatory permission.
Responsibility closure does not prove external legal liability.
Incentive-compatible reports remain reports rather than regulatory evidence.
Public authority cannot be modeled as merely another private contracting party unless the declared formal theory actually gives that semantics.



2. Contract Authority Versus Regulatory Authority
Prompt 20 may establish:
[ \mathsf{ContractAllows}(a). ]
Prompt 21 asks whether the regulatory authority permits, requires, conditions, or prohibits (a).
The theories are independent.
PRO-REG1 — Contract Permission and Regulatory Permission Are Logically Independent
Neither:
[ \mathsf{ContractAllows}(a) \Longrightarrow \mathsf{RegulatorilyPermitted}(a) ]
nor:
[ \mathsf{RegulatorilyPermitted}(a) \Longrightarrow \mathsf{ContractAllows}(a) ]
holds generically.
Proof by two synthetic constructions
Construction A
A private construction contract allows the contractor to remove wall (W).
The effective synthetic regulatory rule prohibits removal of (W).
Thus:
[ \mathsf{ContractAllows}(a)=\mathsf{TRUE}, ]
while:
[ \mathsf{RegulatorilyPermitted}(a)=\mathsf{FALSE}. ]
Construction B
The synthetic regulatory system permits painting a façade element.
The private architectural contract prohibits that change without architect consent.
Thus:
[ \mathsf{RegulatorilyPermitted}(a)=\mathsf{TRUE}, ]
while:
[ \mathsf{ContractAllows}(a)=\mathsf{FALSE}. ]
Therefore neither implication is valid without a bridge. ∎
A project action must satisfy both theories when both govern.

[ \boxed{ \text{safe} \neq \text{formally code compliant}. } ]
[ \boxed{ \text{formally compliant} \neq \text{permit issued}. } ]
[ \boxed{ \text{permit issued} \neq \text{as-built compliant}. } ]
[ \boxed{ \text{inspection passed} \neq \text{universal compliance}. } ]

[ \boxed{ \text{latest published standard} \neq \text{adopted standard}. } ]
[ \boxed{ \text{source authentic} \neq \text{source legally applicable}. } ]
[ \boxed{ \text{citation} \neq \text{incorporation by reference}. } ]
[ \boxed{ \text{rule-internal exception} \neq \text{authority-granted deviation}. } ]
[ \boxed{ \text{engineering equivalence} \neq \text{approved alternative compliance}. } ]
[ \boxed{ \text{appeal available} \neq \text{appeal successful}. } ]
[ \boxed{ \text{absence of a modeled prohibition} \neq \text{proof of legal permission}. } ]



4. Standing Regulatory Theory
Fix:
\left( \Theta_{\mathrm{jurisdiction}}, \Theta_{\mathrm{authority}}, \Theta_{\mathrm{sources}}, \Theta_{\mathrm{adoption}}, \Theta_{\mathrm{applicability}}, \Theta_{\mathrm{precedence}}, \Theta_{\mathrm{exceptions}}, \Theta_{\mathrm{alternatives}}, \Theta_{\mathrm{deviation}}, \Theta_{\mathrm{permit}}, \Theta_{\mathrm{inspection}}, \Theta_{\mathrm{appeal}}, \Theta_{\mathrm{professional}}, \Theta_{\mathrm{evidence}}, \Theta_{\mathrm{release}} \right). } ]
ASSUMP-REG1 — Jurisdiction Identity
Every regulatory claim identifies the exact territorial and institutional jurisdiction.
ASSUMP-REG2 — Authority Identity
Every binding source or decision is connected to an authority competent under the declared formal theory.
ASSUMP-REG3 — Source Authenticity
Every source text, edition, amendment, authority order, permit artifact, or decision relied upon is authentic.
ASSUMP-REG4 — Adoption Correctness
The model correctly represents which source editions have been adopted, enacted, delegated, or incorporated.
ASSUMP-REG5 — Effective-Date Correctness
Effective dates, expiry dates, transition dates, and project cutoffs are represented correctly.
ASSUMP-REG6 — Applicability Completeness
Every rule whose applicability can change a mandatory root claim is represented or explicitly unresolved.
ASSUMP-REG7 — Amendment Completeness
Relevant jurisdictional amendments and project-specific authority orders are represented.
ASSUMP-REG8 — Precedence Correctness
Every override or priority relation used to resolve a conflict is valid in the declared formal theory.
ASSUMP-REG9 — Incorporation Scope
A referenced external standard enters the rule system only to the extent established by the scoped incorporation relation.
ASSUMP-REG10 — Exception Correctness
A rule-internal exception is applied only when its exact source-defined predicate is satisfied.
ASSUMP-REG11 — Deviation Authority
Every variance, waiver, modification, alternative method, equivalency, or other authority-granted deviation is supported by the authority state required by the formal theory.
ASSUMP-REG12 — Permit-State Correctness
Permit submissions, reviews, approvals, denials, expirations, suspensions, conditions, and revisions are represented correctly.
ASSUMP-REG13 — Inspection Scope
Inspection conclusions remain limited to the inspected artifact version, inspected scope, and accepted evidence.
ASSUMP-REG14 — Professional-Attestation Scope
Professional seals and attestations are interpreted only within their declared person, credential, document, claim, and version scope.
ASSUMP-REG15 — Architectural Sovereignty
Regulatory admissibility does not itself choose among several compliant architectural alternatives.
ASSUMP-REG16 — Materialization Identity
Regulatory conclusions refer to the correct Prompt-13 concrete design version.
ASSUMP-REG17 — Physical-Execution Identity
As-built regulatory conclusions use the applicable Prompt-14 field evidence and physical-state version.
ASSUMP-REG18 — Legal-Scope Discipline
Formal regulatory conclusions do not automatically become judicial, enforceability, liability, or legal-advice conclusions.
ASSUMP-REG19 — UNKNOWN Discipline
Unresolved authority, source, applicability, precedence, adoption, permit, inspection, or interpretation questions remain unresolved.
ASSUMP-REG20 — Checker Soundness
Trusted source, arithmetic, rule, permit, inspection, evidence, and release checkers are sound.
ASSUMP-REG21 — Dependency Completeness
Every dependency relevant to an exact incremental regulatory claim is represented.
ASSUMP-REG22 — Regulatory-State Coverage
Whenever robust compliance is claimed, the actual governing authority state belongs to the declared regulatory-state family.
ASSUMP-REG23 — Nonempty Authority Family
The maintained regulatory-state family is nonempty. An empty family is treated as evidence or theory conflict, not vacuous compliance.
ASSUMP-REG24 — Formalization Fidelity
Each formalized rule predicate faithfully represents the source proposition claimed by its certificate.

Define:
\left( \mathsf{territory}, \mathsf{authorities}, t, \mathsf{projectClass}, \mathsf{use}, \mathsf{permitHistory}, \mathsf{projectVersion} \right). } ]

6. Regulatory Sources
DEF-REG2 — Regulatory Source
A Regulatory Source is:
\left( \mathsf{id}, \mathsf{issuer}, \mathsf{instrumentType}, \mathsf{territory}, \mathsf{edition}, \mathsf{effectiveInterval}, \mathsf{scope}, \mathsf{textHash}, \mathsf{provenance}, \mathsf{status} \right). } ]
Instrument types may include:
statute;
administrative regulation;
adopted model code;
local amendment;
incorporated standard;
authority order;
permit condition;
alternative-method decision;
deviation decision;
appeal decision.
No universal hierarchy is assumed.



7. Adoption and Effectiveness
DEF-REG3 — Adoption Certificate
Define:
\left( \mathsf{adoptingAuthority}, \mathsf{source}, \mathsf{edition}, \mathsf{effectiveDate}, \mathsf{territorialScope}, \mathsf{projectScope}, \mathsf{amendments}, \mathsf{evidence} \right). } ]
An adoption certificate is a formal evidence artifact. It does not become authoritative law merely because ANANKE generated it.



DEF-REG4 — Effective Regulatory Source
A source (s) is effective for context (J_t) in exact authority state (L) when:
(s) is authentic;
the required authority or adoption chain exists;
the project lies in the territorial and substantive scope;
the relevant time lies within the applicable effective interval;
no valid supersession or displacement rule removes it;
the project-transition rules select it.
Write:
[ \mathsf{Effective}_L(s,J_t). ]



THM-REG1 — The Latest Published Edition Need Not Be the Governing Adopted Edition
Statement
There exist synthetic regulatory systems in which:
compliance with the adopted edition does not imply compliance with the latest published edition; and
compliance with the latest published edition does not imply compliance with the adopted edition.
Proof
Let synthetic edition (E_1) be adopted.
Let later edition (E_2) be published but unadopted.
First direction
Suppose:
[ E_1:\quad x\ge1, ]
[ E_2:\quad x\ge2. ]
Take:
[ x=1.5. ]
Then:
[ x\models E_1, ]
but:
[ x\not\models E_2. ]
Thus adopted-edition compliance need not imply latest-edition compliance.
Reverse direction
Now suppose:
[ E_1:\quad x\le1, ]
[ E_2:\quad x\le2. ]
Take:
[ x=1.5. ]
Then:
[ x\models E_2, ]
but:
[ x\not\models E_1. ]
Thus latest-edition compliance need not imply adopted-edition compliance.
Therefore:
[ \boxed{ \text{latest published edition} \neq \text{governing adopted edition} } ]
without a valid adoption bridge. ∎



THM-REG2 — Authentic Regulatory Text Does Not Establish Its Applicability to a Target Project
Proof by construction
Let (s) be one authentic synthetic source.
Let its rule apply exactly to projects of class:
[ \mathsf{ClassA}. ]
Project (P_1) has class:
[ \mathsf{ClassA}. ]
Project (P_2) has class:
[ \mathsf{ClassB}. ]
The source bytes, hash, provenance, issuer, and edition are identical for both projects.
Yet:
[ \mathsf{Applies}(s,P_1)=\mathsf{TRUE}, ]
while:
[ \mathsf{Applies}(s,P_2)=\mathsf{FALSE}. ]
Therefore source authenticity alone does not establish target applicability. ∎



8. Regulatory Authority Graph
DEF-REG5 — Regulatory Authority Graph
Define a labeled directed graph:
(V,E,\ell), } ]
where nodes may represent:
authorities;
sources;
editions;
amendments;
decisions;
adopted standards;
permit conditions.
Edge labels may include:
[ { \mathsf{DERIVES_AUTHORITY}, \mathsf{ADOPTS}, \mathsf{AMENDS}, \mathsf{SUPERSEDES}, \mathsf{INCORPORATES}, \mathsf{DELEGATES}, \mathsf{CONDITIONS}, \mathsf{CITES} }. ]
Each edge label has its own formal semantics.
No graph operation is valid merely because it is graph-theoretically convenient.



9. Incorporation by Reference
DEF-REG6 — Scoped Incorporation Relation
Write:
[ \boxed{ s_1 \xrightarrow[\Gamma]{\mathsf{IBR}} s_2 } ]
when source (s_1) incorporates source (s_2) over exact scope (\Gamma).
The relation records where applicable:
incorporated edition;
incorporated sections;
exclusions;
amendments;
whether nested references are included;
effective interval;
project scope.



THM-REG3 — Incorporation by Reference Is Not Generically Transitive
Proof by synthetic counterexample
Let source (A) incorporate source (B) under scope:
\text{“the direct normative clauses of }B\text{, excluding external references.”} ]
Thus:
[ A \xrightarrow[\Gamma_{AB}]{\mathsf{IBR}} B. ]
Let (B) incorporate source (C) for projects directly governed by (B):
[ B \xrightarrow[\Gamma_{BC}]{\mathsf{IBR}} C. ]
Because (\Gamma_{AB}) explicitly excludes external references made by (B), the (A)-to-(B) incorporation does not import (C).
Therefore:
[ A \not\xrightarrow{\mathsf{IBR}} C. ]
We have:
[ A\mathsf{,IBR,}B, \qquad B\mathsf{,IBR,}C, ]
without:
[ A\mathsf{,IBR,}C. ]
Hence generic transitivity fails.
A fortiori, if (B) merely cites (C), no incorporation follows without an additional rule. ∎



10. Regulatory Rules
DEF-REG7 — Regulatory Rule
A regulatory rule is:
\left( s, \mathsf{subject}, \mathsf{trigger}, \mathsf{disposition}, \phi_r, \mathsf{exceptions}, \mathsf{verification}, \mathsf{priority} \right), } ]
where:
[ \mathsf{disposition} \in { \mathsf{REQUIRED}, \mathsf{FORBIDDEN}, \mathsf{CONDITIONAL}, \mathsf{EXPLICITLY_PERMITTED} }. ]
The project predicate:
[ \phi_r ]
contains the formal content of the rule.
The presence of an explicit permission disposition does not imply that every unmentioned action is permitted.



11. Applicability
DEF-REG8 — Applicability Predicate
For rule (r), context (J_t), and artifact (b):
[ \boxed{ \mathsf{Applies}(r,J_t,b) \in { \mathsf{TRUE}, \mathsf{FALSE}, \mathsf{UNKNOWN} }. } ]
A useful exact-state interpretation is:
[ \mathsf{Applies}_L(r,J_t,b) \in {0,1}. ]
For an unresolved family (\mathfrak L_{J_t}):
\begin{cases} \mathsf{TRUE}, & \forall L\in\mathfrak L_{J_t}, ; \mathsf{Applies}L(r,J_t,b)=1, \[4pt] \mathsf{FALSE}, & \forall L\in\mathfrak L{J_t}, ; \mathsf{Applies}_L(r,J_t,b)=0, \[4pt] \mathsf{UNKNOWN}, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} ]
Thus UNKNOWN is a genuine mixed authority-state result.



DEF-REG9 — Applicability Certificate
An applicability certificate contains:
rule ID;
source and edition;
jurisdiction;
project version;
project classifications;
exact applicability inputs;
predicate evaluation;
evidence;
checker version.
A nonapplicability certificate is equally scoped.



PRO-REG2 — Failure to Retrieve an Applicable Rule Does Not Prove Nonapplicability
Proof by construction
Consider two regulatory worlds agreeing on every source retrieved by the system.
In world (W_1), no additional source exists.
In world (W_2), an omitted local amendment exists and applies to the project.
The retrieval output is identical.
The effective rule set differs.
Therefore:
[ \boxed{ \text{rule not retrieved} \not\Longrightarrow \text{rule not applicable}. } ]
∎



12. Effective Regulatory Rule Set
DEF-REG10 — Effective Regulatory Rule Set
For an exact authority state (L), define:
\left{ r: \begin{array}{l} \mathsf{Effective}_L(\mathsf{source}(r),J_t),\ \mathsf{Applies}_L(r,J_t,b)=1,\ r\text{ is not displaced under }L \end{array} \right}. } ]
Under unresolved authority state, ANANKE preserves the family:
[ \left{ \mathcal R_{\mathrm{eff}}(L,J_t,b): L\in\mathfrak L_{J_t} \right}. ]
It does not silently union or intersect the rule sets and call the result “the code.”



13. Formal Regulatory Compliance
DEF-REG11 — Formal Compliance
For exact authority state (L), define:
[ \boxed{ \mathsf{Compliant}L(b;J_t) \iff \forall r\in \mathcal R{\mathrm{eff}}(L,J_t,b), \quad \mathsf{Sat}_L(b,r). } ]
When (\mathfrak L_{J_t}={L}), abbreviate:
[ \mathsf{Compliant}(b;J_t). ]
The satisfaction relation may depend on:
direct compliance;
rule-internal exceptions;
approved alternatives;
valid authority-granted deviations;
project-specific conditions.



PRO-REG3 — Absence of a Modeled Prohibition Does Not Prove Permission
Construction
Let two exact regulatory worlds agree on every modeled source.
World (W_1) contains no additional prohibition on action (a).
World (W_2) contains one omitted applicable prohibition on (a).
The modeled rule base contains no prohibition in either computational state.
Actual permission differs.
Therefore absence of a modeled prohibition cannot establish permission unless the action class carries a separate completeness or explicit-permission certificate. ∎



14. Monotonicity of Pure Conjunctive Obligations
THM-REG4 — Adding Pure Conjunctive Obligations Cannot Enlarge the Formally Compliant Set
Let (X) be a fixed project universe.
For a rule set (R), define:
\left{ b\in X: \forall r\in R, ; \mathsf{Sat}(b,r) \right}. ]
If:
[ R_1\subseteq R_2, ]
then:
[ \boxed{ C(R_2)\subseteq C(R_1). } ]
Proof
Take:
[ b\in C(R_2). ]
Then:
[ \mathsf{Sat}(b,r) ]
for every:
[ r\in R_2. ]
Because:
[ R_1\subseteq R_2, ]
the same holds for every (r\in R_1).
Therefore:
[ b\in C(R_1). ]
Hence:
[ C(R_2)\subseteq C(R_1). ]
∎
This theorem concerns pure conjunction under fixed semantics.
Adding:
an exception;
an alternative route;
a deviation;
a changed interpretation
is not merely adding another conjunctive obligation and may enlarge the admissible set.



15. Rule-Internal Exceptions
DEF-REG12 — Rule-Internal Exception
A rule-internal exception is part of the rule’s own applicability or satisfaction semantics.
For example:
\mathsf{BaseApplies}_L(r,b) \land \neg \mathsf{Exception}_L(r,b). ]
If the exception predicate is satisfied, the base obligation may not apply.
No separate authority-granted deviation is inferred.



16. Authority-Granted Deviations
DEF-REG13 — Authority-Granted Deviation
Use the neutral formal category:
\left( \mathsf{authority}, \mathsf{affectedRule}, \mathsf{project}, \mathsf{scope}, \mathsf{conditions}, \mathsf{effectiveInterval}, \mathsf{evidence}, \mathsf{version} \right). } ]
A real jurisdiction may use labels such as:
variance;
waiver;
modification;
equivalency approval;
exception order;
special approval.
Prompt 21 does not assign a real-world label without authoritative evidence.



THM-REG5 — Rule-Internal Exception and Authority-Granted Deviation Are Logically Distinct
Proof by two synthetic projects
Let base rule (r) require:
[ P(b). ]
It contains rule-internal exception predicate (E(b)).
Project (b_A)
Assume:
[ E(b_A)=\mathsf{TRUE}. ]
No deviation artifact exists.
The base requirement does not apply because the rule’s own exception predicate is satisfied.
Project (b_B)
Assume:
[ E(b_B)=\mathsf{FALSE}, ]
and:
[ P(b_B)=\mathsf{FALSE}. ]
A competent synthetic authority grants deviation (d) modifying the obligation for (b_B).
Project (b_B) becomes formally admissible through (d), not through the rule-internal exception.
Thus:
(b_A) relies on the source’s exception semantics;
(b_B) relies on a project-specific authority act.
The proof objects differ, so the concepts are not identical. ∎



17. Alternative Compliance
DEF-REG14 — Alternative Compliance Proposal
Define:
\left( \mathsf{baseRequirement}, \mathsf{alternativeDesign}, \mathsf{equivalenceClaim}, \mathsf{evidence}, \mathsf{reviewAuthority}, \mathsf{decision} \right). } ]
The proposal separates:
engineering evidence;
the formal rule authorizing an alternative route;
authority acceptance where required.



THM-REG6 — Accepted Alternative Compliance Is Sound Under Its Declared Alternative-Method Rule
Suppose exact regulatory state (L) defines rule satisfaction by:
[ \mathsf{Sat}_L(b,r) \iff P_r(b) \vee \left( A_r(b,e) \land \mathsf{ValidApproval}_L(q) \right). ]
Assume:
[ A_r(b,e)=\mathsf{TRUE} ]
and:
[ \mathsf{ValidApproval}_L(q)=\mathsf{TRUE}. ]
Then:
[ \mathsf{Sat}_L(b,r). ]
Proof
The second disjunct:
[ A_r(b,e) \land \mathsf{ValidApproval}_L(q) ]
is true.
Therefore the disjunction defining (\mathsf{Sat}_L(b,r)) is true. ∎
The theorem is formal and conditional on the alternative-method rule actually existing in the authority state.



THM-REG7 — Engineering Equivalence Alone Does Not Establish Regulatory Acceptance
Construction
Let the engineering checker prove:
[ A_r(b,e)=\mathsf{TRUE}. ]
Suppose the governing formal rule also requires:
[ \mathsf{ValidApproval}_L(q). ]
No authority decision (q) exists.
Then:
[ A_r(b,e)=\mathsf{TRUE}, ]
but:
[ \mathsf{ValidApproval}_L(q)=\mathsf{FALSE}. ]
Therefore:
[ \mathsf{Sat}_L(b,r)=\mathsf{FALSE} ]
under the declared alternative-method semantics.
Thus:
[ \boxed{ \text{engineering equivalence} \not\Longrightarrow \text{formal regulatory acceptance}. } ]
∎



18. Regulatory Conflicts and Precedence
DEF-REG15 — Regulatory Conflict
Rules (r_1,r_2) conflict for project (b) under state (L) when:
both are effective;
both apply;
their dispositions cannot be jointly satisfied.



DEF-REG16 — Regulatory Priority Relation
Write:
[ r_1\succ_{J,L}r_2 ]
when the declared authority theory gives (r_1) priority over (r_2) for the relevant conflict class.
No universal hierarchy is presumed.



THM-REG8 — Deterministic Total Priority Uniquely Resolves a Finite Nonempty Conflict Set
Let (C) be a finite nonempty set of conflicting applicable rules.
Assume:
(\succ) is a strict total order on (C);
the formal resolution rule selects the unique (\succ)-maximal element.
Then the governing rule is unique.
Proof
Because (C) is finite and nonempty, a strict total order on (C) has at least one maximal element.
Suppose (r) and (r') are two distinct maximal elements.
Totality implies either:
[ r\succ r' ]
or:
[ r'\succ r. ]
In the first case (r') is not maximal.
In the second case (r) is not maximal.
Contradiction.
Therefore the maximal element is unique. ∎
This theorem does not prove that a real jurisdiction uses the declared priority relation.

44. Falsification and Regression Suite
Same design, different jurisdiction: identical artifact receives different formal reports.
Adopted versus latest edition: checker must select the adopted edition.
Authentic source, wrong jurisdiction: authenticity passes and applicability fails.
Authentic source, wrong effective date: source is valid but not effective.
Missing adoption certificate: publication alone must not create an effective source.
Citation treated as incorporation: incorrect inference must be rejected.
Scoped incorporation: only included sections become effective.
Local amendment: amended rule replaces the base result under the declared authority semantics.
Incomparable rule conflict: return authority conflict rather than favorable selection.
Applicability TRUE: all exact authority states agree.
Applicability FALSE: all exact states agree on nonapplicability.
Applicability UNKNOWN: exact states disagree.
Missing retrieval: omitted rule must not become nonapplicable.
Pure conjunctive monotonicity: added obligation cannot enlarge compliance set.
Built-in exception: exception predicate correctly removes the base obligation.
Invalid exception: failed predicate cannot be treated as an exception.
Valid authority deviation: competent, scoped, current decision modifies the obligation.
Expired deviation: old decision no longer discharges the current obligation.
Engineering equivalence without approval: remain unapproved.
Approved alternative: both engineering and authority predicates pass.
Multi-jurisdiction intersection: project must pass every required independent jurisdiction.
Robust ambiguity set: compliance under all states.
Possible ambiguity set: compliance under at least one state.
Ambiguity shrink: robust set cannot shrink.
Possible but not robust: checker must retain weaker modality.
Transition-rule difference: same adoption date, different permit-history rule.
Permit replay: versioned process trace reaches exact state.
Formal compliance, permit blocked: missing administrative artifact prevents issuance.
Permit issued, as-built violation: prior issuance does not certify changed field state.
Inspection scope: passed inspection cannot close unrelated rules.
Failed inspection: scoped violation produces failure.
Appeal available, denial affirmed: no reversal.
Appeal changes decision: valid reversal updates the process state.
Attestation without approval: modalities remain separate.
Approval without modeled attestation: reverse independence case.
Formal compliance with omitted hazard: safety claim fails.
Safe but administratively noncompliant: regulatory claim fails.
Conflict core: exact infeasible rule subset is recovered.
Hitting-set repair benchmark: exact minimum repair is recovered.
Prompt-12 sovereignty: regulatorily equivalent designs retain human architectural choice.
Prompt-13 rematerialization: detailed design change reopens compliance.
Prompt-14 field deviation: as-built change invalidates design-only compliance.
Prompt-18 economic infeasibility: regulatory repair exists physically but cannot currently be executed.
Prompt-19 deadline: appeal or submission after expiry is rejected.
Prompt-20 authority: unauthorized party cannot validly file or approve the action.
Prompt-10 breaker: omitted local amendment breaks the compliance claim.
Incremental versus cold: exact agreement after source or design change.
AI compliance argument: attractive but uncertified interpretation is rejected.
PCRJ independence: checker verifies the package without trusting the proposal generator.

def EffectiveRules
    (L : RegulatoryState)
    (J : RegulatoryContext)
    (b : ConcreteArtifact) :

    (L : RegulatoryState)

    (Ls : Set RegulatoryState)
    (J : RegulatoryContext)

    (Ls : Set RegulatoryState)
    (J : RegulatoryContext)
    (b : ConcreteArtifact) : Prop :=

    (Ls : Set RegulatoryState)
    (LActual : RegulatoryState)
    (hActual : LActual ∈ Ls)

55. What Has Now Been Proven
Jurisdiction semantics
Formal regulatory status is jurisdiction specific.
The same physical artifact may have different formal regulatory statuses in different jurisdictions.
Contract permission and regulatory permission are logically independent.
Regulatory analysis requires explicit project and jurisdiction identity.
Regulatory-source provenance
Source authenticity is distinct from applicability.
Every exact effective rule requires a source-provenance path.
Failure to retrieve a source does not prove nonapplicability.
Absence of a modeled prohibition does not prove permission.
Adoption and editions
The latest published edition need not be the adopted edition.
Compliance with an adopted edition need not imply compliance with a newer publication.
Compliance with a newer publication need not imply compliance with the adopted edition.
Adoption must be supported by a scoped authority artifact.
Adoption date alone does not determine transition applicability.
Incorporation by reference
Incorporation is scoped.
Incorporated editions and sections must be explicit where required.
Incorporation is not generically transitive.
Citation does not create incorporation without an authority rule.
Rule applicability
Applicability is project, context, source, edition, and authority-state dependent.
Applicability can be TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN.
UNKNOWN applicability is not nonapplicability.
Exact effective rule sets should be preserved by authority state when unresolved.
Rule-set monotonicity
Under fixed semantics, adding pure conjunctive obligations cannot enlarge the compliant set.
Exceptions, deviations, and alternatives are not merely additional conjunctive obligations.
Exceptions
A rule-internal exception belongs to the rule’s own applicability or satisfaction semantics.
An exception is distinct from a project-specific authority-granted deviation.
An exception requires its exact predicate.
Authority-granted deviations
A deviation requires competent authority, project scope, conditions, evidence, and version.
A deviation is not automatically permanent.
An expired deviation does not discharge a current obligation.
Alternative compliance
An accepted alternative route can formally satisfy a rule under an explicit alternative-method rule.
Engineering equivalence alone does not establish regulatory acceptance.
Authority approval and engineering evidence remain separate inputs.
Rule conflicts and precedence
A finite conflict set with a valid strict total priority relation has one unique governing rule.
Incomparable active conflicting rules remain unresolved.
ANANKE may not choose the interpretation favorable to compliance without authority.
Multi-jurisdiction projects
Independent mandatory jurisdictions compose through set intersection.
Passing one required jurisdiction does not imply passing every required jurisdiction.
Regulatory ambiguity
A regulatory authority-state family preserves unresolved interpretations and applicability.
Robust compliance across the family applies to the actual state when the actual state is covered.
Possible compliance does not establish actual compliance.
Shrinking the authority-state family enlarges the robustly admissible set.
Shrinking the authority-state family shrinks the merely possible set.
Regulatory uncertainty should not be averaged into one “compliance probability” without a separate probabilistic model.
Transitional semantics
Project applicability may depend on permit history and transition rules.
Identical adoption dates can produce different governing editions under different transition rules.
Permits
Permit state is a process-state proposition.
Formal design compliance does not imply permit issuance.
Permit issuance does not imply future as-built compliance.
Permit conditions are project-specific regulatory dependencies where formally valid.
Inspections
Inspection evidence is artifact-version and scope specific.
A scoped inspection pass does not establish universal compliance.
Uninspected obligations remain separately open.
Appeals
An appeal is a procedural option.
Appeal availability does not imply reversal.
Appeal outcomes update the formal process only through valid transitions.
Professional attestations
Professional attestations have exact person, credential, claim, artifact, and version scope.
Professional attestation does not imply authority approval.
Authority approval does not generically imply the modeled professional attestation.
Neither proposition is automatically a legal-liability conclusion.
Compliance versus safety
Formal regulatory compliance does not imply universal engineering safety.
Engineering safety does not generically imply formal regulatory compliance.
Prompt-17 reliability remains distinct from regulatory compliance.
Prompt-14 as-built conformance remains distinct from permit issuance.
Regulatory conflict cores
A regulatory conflict core proves joint infeasibility of the represented rule set and design family.
A conflict core does not select which requirement should change.
Repair hardness
Minimum-cost regulatory repair is NP-hard in the declared hitting-set abstraction.
A valid repair proposal still requires physical, economic, authority, and sovereignty checks.
Incremental recertification
Dependency-directed regulatory recertification equals cold checking under complete dependencies.
Unaffected source and compliance branches may be reused.
Changed editions, amendments, products, classifications, permit conditions, or field states reopen exactly their dependent claims.
Cross-prompt integration
Prompt 9 schedules regulatory information acquisition.
Prompt 10 can attack wrong jurisdiction, missing amendment, invalid incorporation, and overbroad inspection claims.
Prompt 11 supplies evidence, applicability, assumption, and version semantics.
Prompt 12 preserves architectural choice among compliant alternatives.
Prompt 13 supplies the exact design artifact.
Prompt 14 supplies as-built evidence.
Prompt 15 supplies operational state where continuing regulatory obligations depend on operation.
Prompt 16 governs cross-project transfer of compliance evidence.
Prompt 17 keeps reliability claims probabilistic.
Prompt 18 checks whether regulatory repairs and submissions are economically executable.
Prompt 19 checks permit and appeal deadlines against commitment frontiers.
Prompt 20 verifies that the party exercising a regulatory action has the declared authority.
PCRJ and whole-project assurance
The PCRJ stores authority, source, edition, amendment, incorporation, applicability, permit, inspection, appeal, and release evidence.
A checked release witness proves a nonempty release fiber under its exact modality.
A possible release path is not an authority-confirmed release.
Robust compliance is valid for the actual authority state only when that state is covered.
PCRJ checking is linear in explicit proof-DAG size plus local checker costs.
Proposal-source identity does not alter the meaning of an accepted PCRJ certificate.
No formal regulatory result is promoted to external legal liability or enforceability without a separate authoritative bridge.

The jurisdiction law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Regulatory truth is jurisdiction specific. The same physical artifact can have different formal status under different authority states.} } ]
The source law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{No regulatory requirement becomes authoritative merely because ANANKE found text that resembles a code provision. Authority, adoption, version, scope, and applicability must all be carried.} } ]
The edition law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{The governing edition is the edition established by the authority and transition theory—not automatically the newest publication.} } ]
The incorporation law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A reference imports only what the governing incorporation semantics actually incorporates. Regulatory obligations do not propagate through arbitrary citation graphs.} } ]
The applicability law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{An authentic rule affects the target project only through a checked applicability relation. UNKNOWN applicability is not nonapplicability.} } ]
The amendment law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Local amendments and authority decisions are part of the governing theory, not optional annotations on a model source.} } ]
The conflict law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{When active regulatory commands conflict, ANANKE may resolve them only through an authority rule that licenses the resolution. Otherwise the correct result is unresolved conflict.} } ]
The exception law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A rule-internal exception changes the rule's own effect. It is not the same object as an authority-granted deviation from an otherwise applicable obligation.} } ]
The alternative-method law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Engineering equivalence can support an alternative-compliance argument; it does not create regulatory acceptance when the governing theory requires authority approval.} } ]
The ambiguity law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{When several authority interpretations remain possible, preserve the family. Do not select the interpretation that makes the design pass.} } ]
The permit law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Formal design compliance and permit issuance are different propositions: one concerns project obligations, and the other concerns a transition in an authority process.} } ]
The inspection law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{An inspection certificate proves only the inspected claims, on the inspected artifact version, under the evidence actually collected.} } ]
The execution law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Prior approval cannot certify a later physical state that materially departed from the approved artifact.} } ]
The appeal law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{The existence of an appeal preserves a procedural option; it does not predetermine the reviewing authority's decision.} } ]
The professional-attestation law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Professional attestation, regulatory approval, physical truth, contractual responsibility, and legal liability are separate proof modalities.} } ]
The safety law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Formal regulatory compliance is not a substitute for engineering safety analysis, and engineering safety is not a substitute for formal regulatory compliance.} } ]
The sovereignty law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{When several designs are equally regulatorily admissible, the regulator's acceptance does not silently erase the architect's protected choice among them.} } ]
The legal-boundary law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A proof-carrying regulatory model proves exactly its formal jurisdictional proposition. It does not become a court, legislature, regulator, or attorney merely because its proof graph is internally consistent.} } ]
The open-world law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{No closed regulatory theory proves that an omitted binding authority, amendment, interpretation, condition, or legal doctrine does not exist.} } ]
The deepest Prompt-21 principle is:
[ \boxed{ \begin{minipage}{0.91\linewidth} ANANKE becomes a genuine regulatory reasoning system only when every compliance claim carries not merely a rule predicate, but the authority chain that makes the rule relevant: jurisdiction, source identity, adoption, edition, amendment, incorporation, applicability, exceptions, approved deviations, permit history, inspection scope, evidence, and unresolved interpretation. [ e_1,e_2,e_3. ]
A logger records only:
[ e_1,e_3 ]
and computes a valid chain over those two records.
The resulting chain is internally consistent.
No post-record modification occurred.
Event (e_2) is absent.

[ \boxed{ \text{hash-chain consistency} \not\Longrightarrow \text{event completeness}. } ]

48. Synthetic Worked Examples
Every system, value, identity, and event below is synthetic.
Example A — Authentication Without Authorization
Principal Alice authenticates using a valid credential.
Alice is permitted to read plant status.
Alice is not permitted to rewrite elevator-control firmware.
Authentication succeeds.
Authorization denies the firmware action.



Example B — Valid Signature, False Proposition
A credential-valid sensor controller signs:
Valve V is closed.
Physical inspection establishes that (V) is open.
The signature proves the bytes came through the accepted signing path under the key theory.
It does not make the proposition true.



Example C — Replay
A signed command:
[ \mathsf{OPEN} ]
is accepted at sequence (1).
The receiver stores no sequence state.
The same valid bytes are sent again.
The receiver accepts them again.
Adding a monotonic counter permits the second copy to be classified as replay.



Example D — Least Privilege Versus Emergency Safety
An emergency override privilege allows one operator to enter safe shutdown during a hazardous plant state.
Removing the privilege reduces ordinary attack surface.
It also makes emergency safety unreachable.
The correct policy problem is not:
[ \text{minimize permission count}. ]
It is:
[ \text{minimize permissions subject to required operational and safety traces}. ]



Example E — Finite Hash Collision
Use toy hash:
[ H: {m_1,m_2,m_3,m_4,m_5} \rightarrow {00,01,10,11}. ]
Five messages map to four outputs.
At least two messages share a digest.



Example F — Secure Boot
Synthetic chain:
[ B_0\rightarrow B_1\rightarrow B_2. ]
Each stage verifies the next against an allowlist.
THM-SEC8 proves all executed stages are authorized.
Image (B_2) nevertheless contains a synthetic logic defect.
Boot authorization remains valid.
Runtime security fails.



Example G — Anti-Rollback
Current version:
[ 2. ]
Install valid version:
[ 5. ]
Trusted counter becomes:
[ 5. ]
Later, signed version:
[ 3 ]
is presented.
Signature passes.
Version policy rejects because:
[ 3<5. ]



Example H — Incomplete SBOM
Actual dependencies:
[ {A,B,C}. ]
SBOM lists:
[ {A,B}. ]
The absence of (C) from the SBOM is not proof that (C) is absent from the artifact.



Example I — Reproducible but Malicious Build
Two clean build machines use the same compromised deterministic compiler.
Both produce identical malicious artifact (M).
Reproducibility passes.
Toolchain benignity fails.



Example J — Deterministic Noninterference
States contain:
[ (h,\ell), ]
where (h) is high and (\ell) is low.
Low observer sees only (\ell).
High-only action changes (h) and leaves (\ell) unchanged.
Low action updates (\ell) independently of (h).
Output consistency, low-step consistency, and local respect hold.
THM-SEC15 proves high-only actions cannot affect low observations.



Example K — Authenticated Bad Sensor
Physical value:
[ 20. ]
Compromised but credential-valid sensor reports:
[ 75. ]
The message authenticates.
The physical measurement claim fails.



Example L — Byzantine Majority
Let:
[ n=5, \qquad f=2. ]
Three honest unique sensors report bit (1).
Two Byzantine sensors report (0).
Because:
[ 5\ge2(2)+1, ]
majority returns (1).



Example M — Sybil Failure
Three honest physical sensors have three identities.
One malicious physical device acquires four accepted logical identities.
The malicious device controls the counted majority.
The identity-uniqueness premise fails.
No majority certificate is valid.



Example N — Authorized but Unsafe Actuation
An authenticated, authorized operator requests:
[ \mathsf{PumpOff}. ]
The current physical state has no active backup pressure path.
Authorization passes.
Physical guard rejects.



Example O — Security and Safety Independence
Safe but insecure
A protected safety controller keeps every physical state safe.
A data channel leaks occupancy records.
Secure but unsafe
An isolated authenticated controller runs defective pressure logic.
No cyber attack occurs.
Physical failure occurs.



Example P — Hash-Chained Log Omission
Actual events:
[ e_1,e_2,e_3. ]
Logger records only:
[ e_1,e_3. ]
Its chain is valid over those entries.
The log is tamper consistent and incomplete.



Example Q — Physical Recovery Without Trust Recovery
A compromised credential shuts down a synthetic plant.
An operator manually restarts the plant.
The compromised credential remains active.
Physical operation returns.
Cyber trust does not.

50. Falsification and Regression Suite
Authentication without authorization: authenticated principal cannot perform an ungranted action.
Wrong project role: valid credential in one project context must not transfer authority automatically.
Valid signature over false content: signature passes and semantic proposition fails.
Revoked credential: cryptographic verification may pass while current authentication fails.
Digest mismatch: changed artifact must fail exact digest comparison.
Toy collision: distinct messages share a finite toy digest.
Replay without freshness: valid message executes twice.
Replay with counter: second message is rejected.
Permission reduction: authorized trace set shrinks or remains equal.
Emergency privilege loss: reduced privilege destroys a required safe trace.
Verified boot: authorized chain executes.
Unauthorized image: boot chain rejects.
Authorized defective image: runtime property fails after valid boot.
Attestation limitation: measured state is correct while application behavior fails.
Anti-rollback: lower version is rejected.
Signed older image: signature passes and rollback policy denies.
Complete SBOM: every actual dependency satisfies the declared policy.
Incomplete SBOM: omitted dependency remains possible.
Reproducible benign build: identical inputs give identical output.
Reproducible compromised-toolchain build: reproducibility does not establish benignity.
Provenance invalidation: changed compiler invalidates dependent artifact claims.
Unwinding benchmark: finite machine satisfies noninterference theorem.
Governed declassification: allowed release does not count as a violation.
Local-respect failure: high-only action changes low output and yields a counterexample.
Threat-family enlargement: robustly secure set cannot enlarge.
Dynamic compromise order: equal terminal compromise set, different accepted-command history.
Minimal attack sets: every exhaustive successful state contains one.
Hardening benchmark: recover a known weighted hitting-set optimum.
Authenticated bad sensor: origin authentic, physical value wrong.
Byzantine majority: (n=2f+1) and honest agreement recover true bit.
Byzantine threshold violation: insufficient honest majority remains unresolved.
Sybil attack on identity count: quorum certificate is rejected.
Authorized actuator guard: unsafe command is blocked.
Invariant induction: all finite covered traces remain safe.
Secure but unsafe: security roots hold and physical safety fails.
Safe but confidentiality insecure: physical safety holds and secrecy fails.
Fail-safe versus fail-secure: unconditional fallback cannot satisfy both.
Security-augmented ODT containment: actual state remains in the enlarged set.
Sensor-compromise expansion: ODT uncertainty widens after compromise hypothesis.
Active security lease: claims hold through certified horizon.
Lease invalidation: key compromise reopens dependent claims.
Physical recovery without trust recovery: service resumes while credential remains compromised.
Incident response: state reaches rekeyed and reattested release only after all obligations.
Hash-chain modification: changed anchored entry requires a collision to remain undetected.
Hash-chain omission: internally valid log omits one event.
Circular trust: two mutually attesting components do not form an independent root.
Prompt-11 evidence: signed evidence still requires semantic applicability and scope.
Prompt-14 version mismatch: field device version differs from approved materialization.
Prompt-15 compromised sensor: ODT reopens physical-state uncertainty.
Prompt-17 compromise probability: remains probabilistic rather than deterministic.
Prompt-18 update infeasibility: valid patch plan fails resource or cash constraints.
Prompt-19 deadline: update cannot be committed after its viable window.
Prompt-20 authority: authenticated user lacks governance right.
Prompt-21 authority: cyber permission lacks regulatory authority.
Prompt-10 trust-root breaker: omitted compromised root breaks release.
Incremental versus cold: exact agreement after key, firmware, or policy change.
Malicious proposal: AI-proposed configuration with failed invariant is rejected.
PCSEC independence: checker validates without trusting proposal-generation internals.

    (P₁ P₂ : AuthorizationPolicy)

Low equivalence and noninterference
def LowEquivalent
    (s t : State) : Prop :=
  lowProjection s =
  lowProjection t

def PurgeLow :
    List Action →
    List Action
  | [] => []
  | a :: rest =>
      if IsLow a then
        a :: PurgeLow rest
      else
        PurgeLow rest

def Noninterference
    (sys : DeterministicSystem) : Prop :=
  ∀ s t actions,
    LowEquivalent s t →
    lowObserve
      (executeWord sys s actions)
    =
    lowObserve
      (executeWord sys t
        (PurgeLow actions))

Identity
A principal is distinct from an identifier and credential.

Capability attenuation is monotone under complete mediation.

The authorization law is:

The capability law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A capability is safe only relative to its exact rights, validity, delegation, revocation, context, and complete mediation. Possessing capability bytes is not unlimited authority.} } ]
The cryptographic law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Cryptography establishes precisely scoped computational properties under declared assumptions. It does not convert bytes into physical truth.} } ]
The hash law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A finite digest is a compact cryptographic identifier, not a mathematically injective representation of an unrestricted message universe.} } ]
The signature law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A valid signature can support origin and integrity under the key theory; it cannot prove that the signer was correct, honest, safe, or authorized for the proposition.} } ]
The freshness law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A message may be authentic and intact while being dangerously stale. Replay resistance requires explicit freshness state.} } ]
The boot law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Secure boot restricts which software begins execution. It does not prove that accepted software behaves securely after execution begins.} } ]
The update law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A secure update is a state transition over identity, authorization, version, compatibility, migration, and rollback policy—not merely a signed file transfer.} } ]

The reproducibility law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Reproducibility proves consistency of a declared build process. It does not prove that the source or toolchain being reproduced is benign.} } ]
The information-flow law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Confidentiality is a property of what low-observable behavior can reveal about protected state—not merely whether files are encrypted at rest.} } ]
The threat-model law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Security is always relative to adversary capability. Enlarging the attacker can invalidate a certificate without changing a single line of system code.} } ]
The sensor law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Authentication can establish which sensor sent a value. It cannot establish that the physical world actually has that value.} } ]

61. What Has Now Been Proven
Security versus privacy
Cyber authorization does not imply privacy-permitted use.
Confidentiality does not imply purpose limitation.
Secure transport does not imply legitimate collection or disclosure.
Prompt-22 identity and integrity claims remain inputs rather than substitutes for privacy authority.
Data identity
Privacy claims require exact dataset, model, summary, copy, and version identity.
A model is itself a potentially governed derived artifact.
A privacy certificate for one artifact does not silently transfer to another version.
Purpose limitation
Data use is indexed by actor, data, purpose, operation, recipient, time, and state.
Permission for one purpose does not imply permission for another.
Purpose drift is a trace property.
Joining or training can create purpose drift even without a new raw-data read.
Consent and authority
Consent is a scoped authority artifact.
Consent is not generically necessary under every formal privacy theory.
Consent is not generically sufficient for every operation.
Consent scope includes data, purpose, operation, recipient, time, and revocation.
Privacy authority remains distinct from cyber access.
Revocation
Revocation changes future authority.
Revocation does not make a completed disclosure never have occurred.
Revocation may trigger future deletion or nonuse obligations only under the declared theory.
Retention
Retention is a versioned governance state.
Retention expiry does not prove physical deletion.
A valid hold can alter the active retention state.
Collection authority does not automatically authorize indefinite retention.
Lineage
Data lineage includes copies, joins, aggregates, models, checkpoints, caches, and exports.
Deleting a source does not delete descendants.
Versioned time expansion permits an acyclic lineage representation for evolving systems.
An omitted copy invalidates exact deletion-closure claims.
Deletion closure
Complete lineage plus verified terminal descendant states establishes modeled deletion closure.
Deletion closure is policy relative.
Some descendants may require deletion.
Other descendants may require restriction, aggregation, unlinking, or unlearning.
Physical deletion remains an execution claim.
Model forgetting
Source-data deletion does not alter an already-trained model by itself.
A retained model may remain a descendant of deleted data.
Model forgetting requires a model-level transition or a theorem establishing irrelevance.
Exact unlearning
Exact unlearning is equality with retraining on the deleted dataset.
Exact equality transfers every deterministic downstream report.
The theorem does not prove arbitrary unlearning algorithms exact.
Approximate unlearning requires a separate approximation theorem.
Contextual data minimization
Purpose-contextual data equivalence is an equivalence relation.
Every admitted computation factors through the canonical purpose quotient.
The quotient is the coarsest exact sufficient representation.
Any other exact sufficient representation distinguishes at least as many data states.
Raw distinctions inside one quotient class add no admitted computational capability.
The result is purpose relative.
A future unmodeled purpose may require discarded distinctions.
Selective disclosure
Deterministic selective disclosure induces a partition no finer than raw disclosure.
Releasing a predicate can preserve fewer distinctions than releasing the raw value.
Selective disclosure does not automatically prevent auxiliary linkage.
Pseudonymization
Pseudonymization removes or separates one direct-identifier channel.
Pseudonymization does not imply anonymity.
Remaining attributes may support linkage.
Token secrecy and dataset anonymity are distinct claims.
(k)-anonymity
(k)-anonymity is relative to a declared quasi-identifier set.
(k)-anonymity does not prevent homogeneous sensitive-attribute disclosure.
Quasi-identifier omission can invalidate the certificate.
(k)-anonymity is not differential privacy.
Auxiliary information
Reidentification candidate sets depend on side information.
Stronger auxiliary information can collapse an anonymity set.
Anonymity is auxiliary-information-model scoped.
Unmodeled future public data may invalidate a current inference claim.
Secure aggregation
Secure aggregation may protect intermediate contributions.
Exact aggregate output can still reveal an individual contribution.
Knowing (n-1) contributions determines the final contribution from an exact sum.
Protocol confidentiality and output privacy are separate roots.
Federated analytics
Keeping raw data local does not establish output privacy.
Federated gradients, updates, and summaries can remain revealing.
Federation is an architecture, not a privacy theorem.
Privacy units
Privacy parameters require a declared protected unit.
Event-level, person-level, organization-level, and project-level privacy are distinct.
Group privacy may degrade an event-level bound for a multi-event principal.
Cross-project privacy and individual privacy can coexist with different adjacency relations.
Differential privacy
((\varepsilon,\delta))-DP is a distributional comparison over ordered neighboring pairs.
(\varepsilon) is not an identification probability.
(\delta) is not generically an identification probability.
The neighbor relation is part of the theorem.
Mechanism identity is part of the theorem.
DP post-processing
Deterministic post-processing preserves ((\varepsilon,\delta))-DP.
Post-processing does not repair a wrong privacy unit.
Post-processing does not repair an incomplete accountant.
DP sequential composition
Adaptive two-stage pure-DP composition adds (\varepsilon).
Finite multistage pure composition follows by induction.
Repeated releases create cumulative obligations.
DP parallel composition
Disjoint privacy-unit composition uses the maximum (\varepsilon) under product-form randomness.
Shared random state can invalidate naïve parallel composition.
Data disjointness alone is insufficient when one output reveals another mechanism’s random mask.
Group privacy
A length-(k) neighboring path yields a (k\varepsilon) pure-DP bound.
Event privacy does not silently become equal-parameter person privacy.
DP disclosure limitation
A DP mechanism may reveal the true input with probability above one half.
Differential privacy does not mean zero information.
Differential privacy does not mean no inference.
Exact finite DP checking
The maximum eventwise DP violation equals a positive-part sum.
Finite ((\varepsilon,\delta))-DP can be checked exactly over all ordered neighboring pairs.
A failed checker can return a maximizing event and dataset pair.
Explicit checking is linear in neighbor-pair count times output count, aside from arithmetic cost.
Privacy budgets
Basic pure-DP accounting sums (\varepsilon).
Basic cumulative use is monotone.
Passage of time does not replenish the basic budget.
A different accountant requires a different theorem and version.
Privacy-aware ODT
An ODT can preserve admitted computations through a purpose-sufficient view.
Raw identity is unnecessary when every operational computation factors through an identity-free quotient.
A separate purpose may retain identity under separate authority.
ODT minimization is purpose and version specific.
Private fleet learning
Fleet transfer requires both Prompt-16 validity and Prompt-23 privacy authority.
Project-level privacy does not automatically protect persons.
Person-level privacy does not automatically protect an entire organization’s participation.
Secure aggregation is not enough without output analysis.
Data-governance execution
A formal governance state does not prove physical deletion.
A formal nondisclosure rule does not prove no external copy exists.
Prompt-14 and Prompt-22 evidence may be required for execution-level claims.
Privacy conflict cores
Privacy, utility, purpose, retention, and budget constraints may be jointly infeasible.
A conflict core identifies incompatibility, not the authorized repair.
Repair hardness
Minimum-cost repair is NP-hard in the finite inference-path abstraction.
A verified nonminimum repair may still be useful.
Privacy repairs can trade among utility, cost, latency, authority, and privacy.
Incremental recertification
Dependency-directed privacy checking equals cold checking under complete dependencies.
Consent, purpose, dataset, model, recipient, or accountant changes invalidate exact descendants.
Unaffected claims may be reused after version and applicability checking.
Cross-prompt integration
Prompt 9 schedules privacy investigations and computations.
Prompt 10 supplies hidden-copy, linkage, purpose-drift, and budget breakers.
Prompt 11 supplies typed evidence and assurance composition.
Prompt 12 remains authoritative over human and architectural sovereignty.
Prompt 13 binds privacy claims to concrete systems and products where relevant.
Prompt 14 supplies physical deletion and execution evidence.
Prompt 15 supplies the operational-twin computation family.
Prompt 16 controls cross-project transfer modality.
Prompt 17 keeps privacy-risk probabilities probabilistic.
Prompt 18 verifies economic feasibility of privacy repairs.
Prompt 19 controls retention, deletion, and release timing.
Prompt 20 governs organizational privacy authority.
Prompt 21 preserves the legal and regulatory boundary.
Prompt 22 supplies confidentiality, integrity, identity, provenance, and threat assumptions.
PCPDG and whole-project release
PCPDG contains purpose, consent, lineage, retention, deletion, unlearning, minimization, inference, DP, ODT, and fleet state.
A checked privacy-release witness proves a nonempty release fiber under its exact modality.
Pseudonymization remains pseudonymization.
(k)-anonymity remains (k)-anonymity.
Differential privacy retains its privacy unit and parameters.
Secure aggregation remains separate from output privacy.
Proposal-source intelligence does not alter certificate semantics.
Explicit PCPDG verification is linear in proof-DAG size plus local checker costs.
No PCPDG proves absence of an auxiliary dataset or hidden copy outside its theory.

The security/privacy law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Cybersecurity governs who can access or alter information under a threat model. Privacy additionally governs whether the information should be collected, used, retained, inferred from, or disclosed for the declared purpose.} } ]
The purpose law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Permission to use information is purpose scoped. Authority for one computation does not silently authorize another.} } ]
The consent law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Consent is a scoped authority artifact inside the formal governance theory—not a universal permission token and not the only possible source of authority.} } ]
The revocation law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Revocation can change future permitted use. It cannot mathematically make a completed past disclosure never have occurred.} } ]
The retention law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A retention deadline changes the governance state. Actual deletion requires an execution and lineage claim.} } ]
The lineage law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Data do not disappear merely because their original file was deleted. Privacy deletion must follow the descendants that the policy declares relevant.} } ]
The unlearning law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Deleting training data is not model forgetting. Exact forgetting is established only when the resulting model equals the model that would have been trained without the deleted data under the declared training semantics.} } ]
The minimization law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{For a fixed purpose, the mathematically strongest form of data minimization is to retain only the coarsest quotient that preserves every admitted downstream computation.} } ]
The selective-disclosure law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{When a purpose requires only a predicate or quotient of an attribute, revealing the full attribute preserves distinctions the purpose does not require.} } ]
The pseudonymization law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Removing direct identifiers changes one linkage channel. It does not prove that remaining attributes cannot identify the same principal through another channel.} } ]
The anonymity law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Anonymity is always relative to what an observer can combine with the release. An auxiliary-information model is part of the claim.} } ]
The aggregation law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Secure aggregation can hide contributions during computation while the released aggregate itself remains highly revealing. Cryptographic confidentiality and statistical privacy are separate proof obligations.} } ]
The privacy-unit law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A privacy parameter is meaningless without specifying what one neighboring change represents. Event privacy, person privacy, organization privacy, and project privacy are different theorems.} } ]
The differential-privacy law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Differential privacy bounds how much the output distribution can change when one protected unit changes. It does not promise that the output contains no information about that unit.} } ]
The composition law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Privacy loss composes across releases. Reusing private data does not reset the proof obligations created by earlier disclosures.} } ]
The ODT law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{An operational twin should retain the information required to operate the building—not every identity-bearing observation from which that operational state happened to be computed.} } ]
The fleet-learning law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Cross-project learning must carry both Prompt-16 transfer semantics and Prompt-23 privacy semantics. A statistically useful fleet dataset is not automatically an authorized or private one.} } ]
The open-world law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{No closed privacy theory proves that an omitted copy, auxiliary dataset, future inference method, hidden recipient, or unknown model dependency does not exist.} } ]
The deepest Prompt-23 principle is:
[ \boxed{ \begin{minipage}{0.91\linewidth} ANANKE becomes a genuine privacy-preserving engineering system only when it treats information distinctions themselves as governed resources. The goal is not merely to hide data from unauthorized attackers. It is to prove which distinctions the admitted purpose actually requires, discard or protect distinctions it does not require, trace every downstream use and derivative, account quantitatively for disclosures, and refuse to infer anonymity, deletion, consent, or privacy more strongly than the lineage, authority, auxiliary-information, and privacy mechanism actually justify. \end{minipage} } ]

Human role
structure HumanRole where
  id : RoleId
  requiredCompetencies : Set CompetencyId
  authority : Set Action
  version : Version
Person-task qualification
def QualifiedFor
    (person : Person)
    (task : HumanTask)
    (state : HumanOperationalState) : Prop :=
  HasRequiredCompetencies person task ∧
  QualificationValid
    person
    task
    state.time ∧
  CurrentTaskFit
    person
    task
    state
Staffing edge
def StaffingEdge
    (task : HumanTask)
    (person : Person)
    (state : HumanOperationalState) : Prop :=
  QualifiedFor person task state
HMI decision sufficiency
def DecisionSufficient
    (display : State → Observation)
    (required : State → Action) : Prop :=
  ∀ x y,
    display x = display y →
    required x = required y
Factorization theorem skeleton
theorem decision_sufficient_iff_factor
    [Nonempty Action]
    (H : State → Observation)
    (a : State → Action) :
    DecisionSufficient H a ↔
    ∃ π : Observation → Action,
      a = π ∘ H := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    -- Define π on the image of H,
    -- extend arbitrarily outside the image,
    -- prove well-definedness from h.
    ...
  · rintro ⟨π, rfl⟩
    intro x y hxy
    simp [hxy]
Workload
structure AttentionTask where
  demand : ℝ
  releaseTime : Time
  deadline : Time

def WorkloadFeasible
    (tasks : Finset AttentionTask)
    (capacity : Time → ℝ)
    (schedule : HumanSchedule) : Prop :=
  ScheduleRespectsTasks tasks schedule ∧
  ∀ t,
    InstantaneousDemand schedule t
      ≤ capacity t

  authority : AuthorityMap

Effective override
def EffectiveOverrideTiming
    (hazardHorizon : Duration)
    (obsMax decisionMax commMax actMax : Duration) : Prop :=
  obsMax + decisionMax + commMax + actMax
    ≤ hazardHorizon

def OverrideImpossibleTiming
    (hazardHorizon : Duration)
    (obsMin decisionMin commMin actMin : Duration) : Prop :=
  hazardHorizon
    <
  obsMin + decisionMin + commMin + actMin

61. What Has Now Been Proven
Authorization versus competence
Authorization and competence are distinct predicates.
Authentication and role authority do not establish technical competence.
An authorized but incompetent person cannot satisfy a competence-bound task assignment.
Training and qualification
Training completion does not establish competence.
Performance assessment may distinguish people with identical training completion.
Competence is task and condition specific.
Qualification is an evidence artifact with scope and validity.
Qualification is not perfect-performance proof.
Current task fitness
A valid qualification does not imply current availability.
A valid qualification does not imply current task-condition compatibility.
Task fitness combines competence, qualification, availability, conditions, and supervision.
Staffing
Human staffing is a qualified assignment problem.
Total headcount is insufficient.
Hall’s condition is necessary and sufficient in the finite unit-capacity model.
A Hall-deficiency set provides an exact structural infeasibility explanation.
Cross-training
Cross-training can add edges to the staffing graph.
Minimum-cost competency-enabling selection is NP-hard in the declared abstraction.
A verified nonminimum training plan may remain valid.
Procedures
A procedure is a state machine with roles, observations, timing, and recovery.
A legal abstract procedure path does not establish human executability.
Human procedure witnesses require staffing, timing, workload, observation, and authority.
Workload
Human attention is treated as a declared finite resource.
Required service above integrated capacity proves infeasibility.
The theorem is structural and does not assert a universal cognitive constant.
Human scheduling
Restricted two-operator task scheduling is weakly NP-hard.
A proposed schedule requires independent verification.
Mean headcount or total labor hours do not alone prove deadline feasibility.
HMI sufficiency
An HMI is decision sufficient exactly when required action is constant on each display fiber.
Decision sufficiency is equivalent to factorization through the HMI.
HMI-indistinguishable states requiring different actions make perfect control impossible.
Human intelligence cannot recover a state distinction absent from the observation model.
Human-decision quotient
Required-action equality defines a human-decision quotient.
The quotient is the coarsest exact representation preserving the decision.
Any exact HMI must distinguish every decision class.
A finite exact interface requires at least (\lceil\log_2m\rceil) ideal binary bits for (m) classes.
Alarm semantics
Alarm identity, source, priority, response, and deadline are separate fields.
Alarm action equivalence is context relative.
The alarm quotient preserves every admitted required response.
Only response-equivalent alarms may be merged exactly.
Alarm overload
Mandatory alarm service above capacity proves incomplete or late response.
Alarm count is not itself decision information.
No universal alarm-rate threshold has been proved.
Human reliability
Independent-step reliability multiplies only under mutual independence.
Equal marginal success rates do not determine joint procedure success.
Probability claims retain their human-performance law and horizon.
Dependence and common cause
Two operators do not automatically create independent redundancy.
Shared procedures can cause perfectly correlated failure.
Team reliability belongs to the joint law.
Personnel duplication does not remove interface or training common causes.
Qualification leases
A qualification lease is time, task, condition, and dependency scoped.
Lease soundness proves formal applicability through the horizon.
It does not prove perfect execution.
Handoffs
A handoff is an information map from outgoing state to receiving state.
Merging states requiring different future actions makes a handoff insufficient.
The handoff quotient is the coarsest exact future-decision-sufficient summary.
A conversation occurring does not establish state preservation.
Team communication
Distributed decisions may require transmission of a decision-separating bit.
Identical local information forces identical deterministic local action.
Missing critical information can make exact coordination impossible.
Human–AI delegation
Delegation requires explicit AI and human action sets.
Approval, veto, escalation, timeouts, information, and authority are separate obligations.
Delegation cannot create authority absent from Prompt 20.
AI cyber authorization cannot create human governance authority.
Human review
Human presence does not repair HMI aliasing.
Human approval does not establish safety when the reviewer lacks decision-sufficient information.
Human review is meaningful only relative to displayed evidence, time, action set, and authority.
Effective override
Override latency requires separate minimum and maximum bounds.
Minimum unavoidable latency beyond the hazard horizon proves override impossibility.
Maximum latency within the horizon plus safe reachability proves robust effectiveness.
An override control’s existence does not establish timeliness.
Physical effect, not merely button activation, must precede the hazard boundary.
Automation-mode awareness
Hidden mode differences can make identical human input have different consequences.
If modes require different decisions, the interface must distinguish them or render them decision equivalent.
Procedure and outcome separation
Procedure conformance does not imply universal success.
Omitted physical disturbances may defeat a correctly executed procedure.
Successful outcome does not imply procedure conformance.
Procedure and outcome require separate evidence roots.
Emergency response
Robust emergency policies are nonanticipative.
Scenario-wise successful plans do not imply one executable policy.
Immediate conflicting actions under indistinguishable scenarios prove nonanticipative infeasibility.
Evacuation
Evacuation is a capacitated population-flow problem.
Exit-cut capacity gives a lower bound on completion time.
Travel-time lower bounds remain additional.
Individually shortest routes need not minimize population makespan.
Congestion can make a longer route system-optimal.
Occupant-class accessibility
Route feasibility is occupant-class relative.
A route usable by one class need not serve another.
Assistance and refuge policies are part of the witness.
Organizational reliability
Individual marginals do not determine team reliability.
Shared procedure revision can defeat personnel redundancy.
Shared HMI, training, supervision, and information can create common cause.
Conflict cores and repairs
Human-operational constraints may be jointly infeasible.
A conflict core identifies the incompatible assumptions.
Repairs may alter staffing, training, HMI, alarms, procedure, automation, or architecture.
Repairs remain subject to Prompt-12 sovereignty.
Incremental recertification
Dependency-directed checking equals cold checking under complete dependencies.
Qualification, HMI, procedure, or staffing changes invalidate descendants.
Unaffected certificates may be reused after scope and version checking.
Prompt integration
Prompt 9 schedules human-factor investigations and measurements.
Prompt 10 supplies HMI, alarm, handoff, workload, and common-cause breakers.
Prompt 11 supplies evidence and assurance composition.
Prompt 12 remains authoritative for architecture and human option sets.
Prompt 13 controls physical access and materialized interfaces.
Prompt 14 supplies evidence of actual procedure execution.
Prompt 15 records human actions in the ODT.
Prompt 16 controls fleet transfer of human-performance evidence.
Prompt 17 keeps human reliability probabilistic.
Prompt 18 verifies staffing, training, and repair affordability.
Prompt 19 controls qualification, preparation, and override deadlines.
Prompt 20 distinguishes incentive alignment from competence.
Prompt 21 distinguishes professional authority from actual performance.
Prompt 22 distinguishes authentication from competence.
Prompt 23 governs human-performance monitoring and evidence use.
PCHO and whole-project release
PCHO contains roles, competence, staffing, procedures, HMI, alarms, handoffs, delegation, overrides, emergency policy, and evacuation.
A checked human-operational witness proves a nonempty execution fiber.
Every accepted claim retains its exact human modality.
Proposal-source intelligence does not alter certificate semantics.
Explicit checking is linear in proof-DAG size plus local checker costs.
No PCHO proves absence of human behavior or organizational causes outside its theory.

The competence law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Human authority to perform an action and human competence to perform it are different proof obligations.} } ]
The training law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Training completion is evidence of participation in training. Competence requires the separate performance proposition the project actually depends on.} } ]
The staffing law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Enough people is not enough. The project requires enough appropriately qualified people for every simultaneously required subset of tasks.} } ]
The procedure law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A procedure becomes operational only when its actions can be assigned to competent people who can observe, understand, authorize, and execute them within the required physical and temporal constraints.} } ]
The workload law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Mandatory human attention is a finite project resource. If required service exceeds the declared capacity of the available people, the procedure is infeasible regardless of how well it is written.} } ]
The HMI law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A human interface is decision sufficient exactly when every pair of physical states it displays identically requires the same human decision.} } ]
The bounded-information law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{No amount of human intelligence can reliably distinguish two project states when the interface presents them as the same observation and the required actions differ.} } ]
The alarm law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Alarm count is not decision information. Preserve the distinctions that change required action and eliminate only distinctions proved operationally equivalent.} } ]
The reliability law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Human-error marginals do not determine team reliability. Shared procedures, interfaces, training, supervision, and environments can create common-cause dependence.} } ]
The handoff law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A handoff is complete only when it preserves every state distinction that can change a receiving team’s required future decision.} } ]
The delegation law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Human–AI delegation is safe only when the division of observation, action, authority, escalation, and timing is explicit and independently checkable.} } ]
The human-in-the-loop law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Adding a human approval step does not create safety when the human lacks decision-sufficient information, adequate time, or an effective action.} } ]
The override law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A human override is real only when the hazard can be observed, understood, decided upon, communicated, and physically altered before the system crosses its irreversible boundary.} } ]
The automation-mode law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{If different automation modes require different human decisions, the interface must expose enough information to distinguish those modes when the distinction matters.} } ]
The conformance law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Procedure conformance and physical success are different propositions. ANANKE must record both rather than infer one from the other.} } ]
The emergency law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A collection of perfect scenario-specific emergency responses is not one executable strategy unless each decision can be made from information actually available at that time.} } ]
The evacuation law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Evacuation is a population-flow problem with capacity, travel time, accessibility, information, and assistance constraints—not merely a collection of individual shortest paths.} } ]
The accessibility law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{The existence of an exit route is meaningful only relative to the occupant class and assistance model for which that route is executable.} } ]
The organizational law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Duplicating people does not duplicate independence when the same erroneous procedure, interface, information source, or organizational assumption can cause them all to fail together.} } ]
The sovereignty law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Reducing human workload does not grant authority to erase protected architecture or human choice. Human-factors repair remains subject to Prompt-12 sovereignty.} } ]
The privacy law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Measuring human performance does not grant unlimited authority to monitor people. Human-operational evidence remains subject to Prompt-23 privacy governance.} } ]
The open-world law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{No closed human-factors theory proves that an omitted behavior, misunderstanding, communication failure, improvisation, or organizational common cause does not exist.} } ]
The deepest Prompt-24 principle is:
[ \boxed{ \begin{minipage}{0.91\linewidth} ANANKE becomes a genuinely executable human–machine project system only when it stops treating people as perfect actuators attached to procedures. Human action must be modeled through competence, information, workload, time, communication, authority, dependence, and physical reachability. The objective is not to predict every human behavior. It is to prove exactly which project procedures remain executable under the declared human-performance model, expose when the interface or staffing makes correct action impossible, and preserve uncertainty wherever real human behavior exceeds the formal theory. \end{minipage} } ]
