68. What Has Now Been Proven
Acceptance-state semantics
Exact structural: Commissioning state is not merely a report; it includes the artifact, requirements, metrology, tests, nonconformances, corrections, latent states, readiness, and versions.
Exact structural: Acceptance is relative to an explicit acceptance basis.
Exact structural: Construction completion, commissioning completion, acceptance, readiness, and handover are distinct states.
Design versus delivered state
Exact negative result: Design compliance does not imply delivered-system acceptance.
Exact structural: Acceptance evidence must bind to the as-built artifact version.
Exact structural: A post-test configuration change can invalidate evidence tied to the test state.
Measurement identity
Exact structural: Every measurement claim requires a measurand identity.
Exact structural: Location, state conditions, units, and version are part of the measurand.
Exact structural: A measurement value without its instrument, conditions, uncertainty, and calibration reference is incomplete.
Measurement uncertainty
Measured bounded: A measurement enclosure contains the true quantity under its declared model.
Exact theorem: Additive bounded errors compose through the triangle inequality.
Exact theorem: Traceability can coexist with nonzero error.
Measured bounded: Bounded drift and noise produce a time-scoped enclosure.
Exact negative result: Expired calibration without a drift model does not establish current validity.
Calibration
Exact structural: Calibration artifacts are versioned, scoped evidence objects.
Exact structural: Calibration chains preserve reference and uncertainty lineage.
Exact negative result: Calibration does not imply exactness.
Time-scoped bounded: Calibration leases preserve validity only through their conditions and horizon.
Guard bands and three-way acceptance
Exact checked: PASS is sound when the entire enclosure lies inside the requirement.
Exact checked: FAIL is sound when the entire enclosure lies outside the requirement.
Exact checked: A boundary-straddling enclosure is unresolved.
Exact theorem: A conservative guard-band pass prevents false acceptance under the declared bound.
Exact limitation: A point estimate inside a limit does not necessarily justify PASS.
Test cases and execution
Exact structural: Test cases include preconditions, stimulus, observations, measurements, acceptance criteria, and restoration.
Exact structural: A test execution artifact binds test version, artifact version, conditions, instrumentation, and evidence.
Exact structural: Test execution and test validity are different claims.
Exact structural: Human-executed tests inherit Prompt-24 competence and workload requirements.
Acceptance observability
Exact theorem: Acceptance can be computed from test outcomes exactly iff acceptance is constant on every test-outcome fiber.
Exact negative result: Test-indistinguishable acceptable and unacceptable states make exact acceptance impossible.
Exact structural: A coverage hole is a pair of states merged by the suite but separated by the acceptance predicate.
Fault coverage
Exact structural: Fault coverage is relative to a declared modeled fault family.
Exact theorem: Adding tests cannot reduce modeled coverage.
Exact theorem: Complete detection of every modeled unacceptable state plus valid all-pass evidence establishes modeled acceptance.
Model scoped: The theorem excludes only modeled covered faults.
Exact limitation: No statement follows about unmodeled defects.
Test-selection hardness
Computational: Minimum-cost complete test selection is NP-hard by Weighted Set Cover.
Exact structural: A verified nonminimum suite may still be correct.
Exact structural: Optimization difficulty does not weaken a verified suite’s coverage certificate.
Operating-envelope coverage
Exact negative result: Passing at one operating point does not establish an unchecked envelope.
Exact structural: Tested domain and required domain must remain explicit.
Exact limitation: Extrapolation requires a separate model-validity theorem.
Fault diagnosis
Exact structural: A fault signature is the complete joint possible test-outcome set.
Exact theorem: Equal signatures prevent guaranteed exact diagnosis.
Exact structural: Diagnostic equivalence classes define the resolution of the current test suite.
Exact limitation: Different repair obligations within one class require additional evidence or a common safe action.
Acceptance sampling
Statistical exact arithmetic: Hypergeometric acceptance probability is exact under uniform sampling without replacement.
Statistical: False acceptance and false rejection are lot-model probabilities.
Exact negative result: A nonexhaustive zero-defect sample can pass a defective lot.
Exact limitation: Statistical acceptance does not establish deterministic lot perfection.
Exact structural: Lot identity and sampling mechanism are part of the claim.
Nonconformance and corrective action
Exact structural: Nonconformance status is versioned and requirement scoped.
Exact structural: Physical rework alone does not close a nonconformance.
Exact negative result: A local retest does not establish global acceptance.
Exact structural: Corrective closure requires physical verification, retest, regression, and version transition.
Regression recertification
Exact structural: Corrective action creates an acceptance regression cone.
Exact theorem: Complete regression recertification restores the same acceptance roots as cold checking.
Exact structural: Unaffected certificates may be reused only through complete dependencies and applicability checks.
Subsystem and integrated-system testing
Exact negative result: Every subsystem may pass while the integrated system fails.
Exact theorem: Complete local guarantees, closed interface assumptions, and global interaction checks establish integrated acceptance.
Exact limitation: Cyclic assume-guarantee reasoning requires a checked invariant or fixed point.
Exact structural: Shared resources, timing, and interactions are system-level acceptance objects.
Latent defects
Exact set-valued: Accepted evidence defines a delivered-state fiber.
Exact theorem: A nonempty defective portion of that fiber blocks exact defect-free status.
Probabilistic: Residual latent-defect risk remains a probability under a declared law.
Exact negative result: Small probability does not mean impossibility.
Open-world: Passing all modeled tests does not exclude defects outside the model.
Test-induced state changes
Exact structural: Commissioning tests are physical and cyber-physical transitions.
Exact negative result: A test result about a temporary state need not apply to the final restored state.
Exact structural: Restoration state and version must be certified.
Commissioning state machines
Exact structural: Commissioning is a stateful transition process.
Exact structural: Test failure, correction, retest, subsystem acceptance, integrated acceptance, readiness, and handover are distinct states.
Exact structural: State transitions require evidence and preconditions.
Punch lists and conditional acceptance
Exact structural: Open items retain requirements, evidence, closure conditions, deadlines, and authority.
Exact negative result: Conditional acceptance does not imply full acceptance.
Authority scoped: Conditional acceptance requires Prompt-20/21 authority.

66. What Has Now Been Proven
Lifecycle-state semantics
EXACT_STATE: Lifecycle state is a versioned object containing configuration, condition, knowledge, degradation, maintenance, support, retrofit, decommissioning, and disposition state.
EXACT_STATE: Prompt-25 handover is the initial lifecycle condition, not a terminal project state.
SET_VALUED: The maintained condition state may be a set rather than a point.
EXACT_STATE: Actual condition and known condition remain distinct.
Acceptance persistence
Exact negative result: Acceptance at (t_0) does not imply integrity at (t_1).
EXACT_STATE: Later integrity refers to the current configuration and condition.
Exact structural: Degradation after handover does not contradict a correct original certificate.
Age versus condition

The renewal law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Renewal mathematics applies only when replacement or repair recreates the renewal state assumed by the model. Imperfect repair must remain imperfect.} } ]
The maintenance law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Maintenance is itself a physical rewrite. It can restore integrity, fail to restore integrity, or create new defects, and every acceptance-relevant maintenance action therefore carries its own evidence and regression obligations.} } ]
The spare law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A repair path is executable only when the required people, parts, support, time, authority, and recertification path exist when the repair is needed.} } ]

[ \boxed{ \textbf{An asset may continue functioning after its support and replacement ecosystem has disappeared. Operability, supportability, availability, and future repairability are distinct lifecycle properties.} } ]
The dependence law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Redundant suppliers or spare paths provide only the reliability justified by their joint dependence structure. Counting vendors is not the same as proving independent availability.} } ]

O \left( N+E+\sum_i c_i \right). } ]

Linear characterization

    (K : Matrix ImpactIndex FlowIndex ℝ)
    (q : FlowIndex → ℝ) :

Characterization additivity

    (K : Matrix ImpactIndex FlowIndex ℝ)
    (q₁ q₂ : FlowIndex → ℝ) :
    Characterize K (q₁ + q₂)
      =

Allocation

  nonnegative :

Time-resolved operational impact

    (load factor : Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ :=

53. What Has Now Been Proven
Environmental-state semantics
EXACT_INVENTORY: Environmental state is versioned and tied to current lifecycle configuration.
Exact structural: Environmental performance is not an immutable property of the original design.
Exact structural: Environmental claims depend on horizon, boundary, service, factors, and lifecycle history.
Functional units
Exact: Functional units contain service quantity, quality, duration, location, and operating conditions.
Exact negative result: Lower absolute burden need not mean lower intensity.
Exact structural: Direct comparison requires functional compatibility or explicit normalization.
UNKNOWN: Unresolved service equivalence blocks exact comparative release.
System boundaries
Exact: Boundary-relative burden includes only represented boundary processes.
Exact theorem: Expanding a nonnegative gross boundary cannot reduce gross burden.
Exact negative result: Signed credits destroy that monotonicity.
Exact structural: Exclusion from a boundary does not prove physical irrelevance.
Inventory
EXACT_INVENTORY: Every accepted flow has identity, quantity, unit, process, time, location, provenance, and version.
Exact structural: Inventory and characterized impact are separate.
UNKNOWN: Missing required flows block complete inventory closure.
Characterization
Exact theorem: Fixed linear characterization is additive.
BOUNDED_IMPACT: Nonnegative box-constrained inventory produces certified interval bounds.
Exact limitation: A characterization factor remains model and version specific.
Exact structural: Inventory completeness does not establish characterization completeness.
Environmental uncertainty
BOUNDED_IMPACT: Inventory and factor sets may produce impact enclosures.
PROBABILISTIC_CLIMATE: Probability laws remain probabilistic.
Exact limitation: Correlation may change attainable impact extremes.

Allocation
Exact: Complete allocation shares conserve total modeled process burden.
Exact negative result: Product-level burden depends on allocation rule.
Exact structural: Allocation changes attribution rather than the shared process total.
Double counting
Exact negative result: Reusing one physical reduction in two claims overstates aggregate reduction.
Exact structural: Event identity is required for portfolio environmental accounting.
Attributional accounting
ATTRIBUTIONAL: Attributional results answer a declared burden-assignment query.
Exact limitation: Attributional accounting does not automatically prove causal consequence.
Consequential accounting
CONSEQUENTIAL: Consequential results depend on a causal response model.
Exact theorem: Attributional and consequential results may differ in sign.
Exact structural: The two modes are not averaged automatically.

Exact theorem: Disjoint lifecycle modules sum to boundary total.
Exact limitation: Overlap creates double counting.
Exact limitation: Omitted modules prevent whole-life closure.

The functional-unit law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Environmental comparison begins by proving that the alternatives provide the service being compared. An impact number without its functional unit is not a complete comparative claim.} } ]

[ \boxed{ \textbf{A system boundary defines what the accounting result includes. It does not make excluded physical processes cease to exist.} } ]

[ \boxed{ \textbf{Every environmental result must be traceable to versioned physical flows with identities, units, times, locations, and provenance.} } ]
The characterization law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Environmental characterization transforms an inventory under a declared model. It does not convert one chosen indicator into universal ecological truth.} } ]
The allocation law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Allocation distributes modeled shared burden among products. Different allocation theories can produce different product results while preserving the same total process burden.} } ]
The attribution law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Attributional accounting asks what burden is assigned to the project under a declared representation. Consequential accounting asks what changes because the project changes. Those are different mathematical queries.} } ]
The whole-life law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Whole-life environmental performance must follow production, construction, operation, maintenance, replacement, retrofit, and end of life without omission or double counting.} } ]
The time law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Environmental intensity can vary with time. Equal energy totals therefore need not produce equal environmental burdens.} } ]
The covariance law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{The error from replacing a time-varying environmental factor with its simple average is governed by the covariance between that factor and project load.} } ]
The counterfactual law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Environmental savings are differences between actual performance and a justified no-intervention counterfactual under comparable conditions—not automatically differences between calendar periods.} } ]
The payback law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Environmental payback occurs only when cumulative avoided burden reaches the burden created by the intervention. Payback on one metric does not establish dominance on every metric.} } ]
The rebound law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Engineering savings and realized environmental savings differ when behavior, operation, service demand, or system response changes after intervention.} } ]
The water law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Water withdrawal, return, storage change, and consumption are different inventory quantities and must not be substituted for one another.} } ]

[ \boxed{ \textbf{A project is robustly climate admissible only when it satisfies the obligation in every surviving scenario. Enlarging the future scenario family can invalidate robustness without changing the building.} } ]

[ \boxed{ \textbf{A gross environmental budget is cumulative. Past burden remains part of the accounting state and cannot be erased by the passage of time.} } ]
The net-zero law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Gross emissions, physical removals, and external balancing credits are distinct quantities. A zero accounting balance must never hide which mechanism produced the zero.} } ]
The circularity law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Material recovery becomes an environmental benefit only through a checked relationship among processing burden, material quality, actual substitution, and displaced production. Mass recovery alone is not the theorem.} } ]
The multi-impact law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Environmental performance is naturally vector valued. When one design is better in one dimension and worse in another, mathematics supplies a Pareto relation—not a hidden universal preference.} } ]
The lifecycle law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Whole-life environmental accounting must follow the actual maintenance, replacement, retrofit, support, and retirement path established by Prompt 26 rather than an imagined lifecycle that cannot occur.} } ]
The open-world law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{No closed environmental model proves that an omitted process, environmental pathway, future climate state, causal response, or substitution effect does not exist.} } ]

[ \sum_{i=1}^{N}c_i. ]
Therefore:
O \left( N+E+\sum_{i=1}^{N}c_i \right). } ]
∎

51. What Has Now Been Proven
Extra-project state semantics
EXACT_INTERFACE: A versioned extra-project state contains projects, interfaces, networks, resources, hazards, externalities, and authority.
Exact structural: Project validity and extra-project validity are separate propositions.
Exact structural: The joint feasible set need not equal the Cartesian product of isolated project sets.
Canonical project interfaces
EXACT_INTERFACE: External interfaces carry withdrawals, injections, service requests, externalities, assumptions, and guarantees.
Exact theorem: Every declared external computation factors through the canonical external quotient.
Exact theorem: Every other exact system-facing representation refines the canonical quotient.
Exact limitation: New regional computations may refine the quotient.
UNKNOWN: Interface omissions block exact extra-project release.
Shared-network conservation
NETWORK_FEASIBLE: Feasible flows satisfy edge capacities and node balance.
Exact structural: Internal network flows cancel when node balances are summed over a region.
Exact structural: Direction and sign conventions are part of every flow claim.
Network cuts
CUT_BOUNDED: Every feasible flow satisfies outward cut capacity.
CUT_BOUNDED: Every feasible flow satisfies incoming cut capacity.
Exact proposition: Negative cut slack proves infeasibility.
Exact limitation: Cut sufficiency is not claimed for arbitrary nonlinear or multi-commodity systems.
Individual versus joint feasibility
Exact negative result: Projects feasible alone may be infeasible together.
PORTFOLIO_FEASIBLE: Joint release requires one shared-system witness.
Exact structural: Local connection adequacy does not prove upstream deliverability.
Pairwise versus global compatibility
Exact negative result: Every pair may be feasible while the whole portfolio is infeasible.
Exact structural: Pairwise certification is not a global certificate.
Portfolio demand and coincident peaks
Exact theorem: Portfolio peak is at least the largest individual peak.
Exact theorem: Portfolio peak is at most the sum of individual peaks.
Exact counterexample: The upper bound may be strict.
Exact structural: Coincidence ratio is portfolio and scenario specific.
UNKNOWN: Stale or misaligned traces block exact coincidence claims.
Demand diversity
Exact structural: Diversity is a temporal relation among multiple projects.
Exact negative result: Local control can destroy diversity.
Exact negative result: Equal project energy does not preserve regional peak.
Average versus peak
Exact theorem: Equal means do not determine equal peaks.
Exact structural: Average utilization cannot size peak-constrained infrastructure alone.
Shared capacity regions
Exact negative result: Individual membership does not imply aggregate membership.
Exact structural: The aggregate portfolio vector must itself satisfy the capacity region.
Project-local versus regional optimization

Exact limitation: Prompt 28 defines no universal scalar social objective.

Exact negative result: A project-local objective need not internalize extra-project cost.

The interface law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A project should expose to shared systems exactly the state distinctions capable of changing extra-project consequences—no fewer for correctness and no more merely because the complete internal model exists.} } ]
The local-versus-global law is:

The pairwise law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Pairwise compatibility does not establish global compatibility when capacity or interaction constraints involve three or more projects simultaneously.} } ]
The cut law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{If demand that must cross an infrastructure cut exceeds that cut's capacity, no downstream rearrangement can make the declared flow feasible.} } ]
The peak law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Regional infrastructure must respond to coincident demand—not to independent peak nameplates and not merely to long-run average demand.} } ]
The diversity law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Demand diversity is a temporal relation among projects, not an intrinsic property of one project. A local control change can create or destroy it.} } ]
The optimization law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Optimizing every project independently does not in general optimize the infrastructure shared by those projects.} } ]
The externality law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A project consequence remains physically real when it crosses the project boundary. Ownership boundaries and causal boundaries are not the same object.} } ]
The higher-order law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{The absence of pairwise harm does not prove the absence of cumulative harm. Some effects exist only when several individually acceptable projects operate together.} } ]
The transfer law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Flows exchanged internally among projects cancel at the portfolio boundary when represented consistently. Internal circulation is not regional resource creation.} } ]
The interdependency law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Infrastructure resilience belongs to the dependency graph, not merely to the number of redundant components visible inside each subsystem.} } ]
The cascade law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A cascade certificate proves closure of the declared dependency rules from the declared initiating state. It does not prove that every real cascade mechanism is represented.} } ]
The common-cause law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Redundancy provides only the resilience justified by its joint dependence structure. Shared upstream infrastructure can erase several nominal protections at once.} } ]
The reachability law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A service configuration can be physically valid as a steady state and still be unreachable from the current degraded state. Recovery requires a transition proof, not merely a feasible endpoint.} } ]
The mutual-aid law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Mutual aid is real only when compatible resources can be allocated, transported, authorized, and delivered before the need expires under the same regional scenario.} } ]
The nonanticipativity law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Regional recovery must act on information available at the time of action. Clairvoyant plans for completed scenarios are not executable preparedness.} } ]
The emergency-capacity law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Low average emergency-service utilization does not certify resilience to simultaneous demand. Deadline feasibility depends on service required inside the critical response window.} } ]
The cumulative-environment law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Environmental admissibility is not preserved automatically under portfolio aggregation. Shared budgets and interaction effects must be checked at the scale where they are defined.} } ]
The scarcity law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{Negative cut slack is structural proof of infrastructure insufficiency. It identifies where the network cannot carry required service without pretending that scarcity is itself a market price.} } ]
The regional-authority law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{A mathematically feasible shared-infrastructure allocation does not create the right to impose that allocation. Governance and regulatory authority remain separate proof layers.} } ]
The open-world law is:
[ \boxed{ \textbf{No closed system-of-systems model proves that an omitted project, utility dependency, externality pathway, common-cause event, regional demand, or recovery obstacle does not exist.} ]

[ v_1,\ldots,v_N. ]

CONJ-SOS1 — Compact External Project Interfaces
Most projects admit external decision-sufficient interfaces much smaller than their complete internal states.
Falsification: regional computations routinely require nearly complete project state.
CONJ-SOS2 — Regional Bottlenecks Have Small Cut Certificates
Many important infrastructure infeasibilities admit small interpretable capacity-cut explanations.
Falsification: practical failures require diffuse certificates spanning most of the network.
CONJ-SOS3 — Peak Diversity Is Material
Portfolio time diversity materially reduces required capacity relative to sum-of-peaks design.
Falsification: relevant project peaks remain consistently coincident.
CONJ-SOS4 — Local Optimization Can Create Material Synchronization
Independent project optimization changes coincident regional peaks enough to matter.
Falsification: project-local controls have negligible system timing effects.
CONJ-SOS5 — Higher-Order Externalities Are Sparse
A moderate family of higher-order interactions captures most cumulative extra-project effects.
Falsification: interaction order grows combinatorially without useful compression.
CONJ-SOS6 — Common-Cause Graphs Remain Manageable
Most high-consequence infrastructure dependence is concentrated in a moderate number of upstream dependencies.
Falsification: dependencies remain extremely diffuse and unstable.
CONJ-SOS7 — Recovery Reachability Exposes Hidden Failures
Dynamic startup analysis discovers important failures missed by static capacity studies.
Falsification: nearly every statically feasible state is operationally reachable.
CONJ-SOS8 — Proof-Carrying Mutual-Aid Assignment Is Useful
Explicit resource, travel, compatibility, and deadline semantics reduce false mutual-aid confidence.
Falsification: aid failures are dominated by unformalized factors.
CONJ-SOS9 — Incremental Regional Recertification Is Sparse
One project change usually reopens only a limited regional dependency slice.
Falsification: routine changes repeatedly require full district analysis.

A 190-room hotel in a realistic synthetic district admits a practical PCSOS.

ADD-SOS28.1 — Experiment-Family Refinement Theorem
Let:
\[ \mathcal F_1\subseteq\mathcal F_2. \]
Define:
\[ x\equiv_{\mathcal F_k}y \iff \forall f\in\mathcal F_k,\quad f(x)=f(y). \]
Then:
\[ \boxed{ x\equiv_{\mathcal F_2}y \Longrightarrow x\equiv_{\mathcal F_1}y. } \]

If \(x\equiv_{\mathcal F_2}y\), every computation in \(\mathcal F_2\) agrees on x,y. Since every computation in \(\mathcal F_1\) also lies in \(\mathcal F_2\), every computation in \(\mathcal F_1\) agrees. Hence:
\[ x\equiv_{\mathcal F_1}y. \]
∎
Therefore an expanded experiment family can split old quotient classes but cannot merge classes that were already distinguished:
\[ \boxed{ \mathcal F_1\subseteq\mathcal F_2 \Longrightarrow Q_{\mathcal F_2} \text{ refines } Q_{\mathcal F_1}. } \]

8. Shared-Resource Allocation
DEF-SOC8 — Shared-Resource Allocation
For n stakeholders:
\[ \boxed{ x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n). } \]
For one divisible resource:
\[ x_i\ge0. \]
Let total available resource be:
\[ C\ge0. \]
DEF-SOC9 — Stakeholder Resource Bounds
For every stakeholder:
\[ \boxed{ \ell_i\le x_i\le u_i, } \]
where:
\(\ell_i\): minimum service or resource floor;
ui: upper bound.
THM-SOC5 — Exact Feasibility of a Bounded Shared-Resource Allocation
Statement
Assume finite n and:
\[ 0\le\ell_i\le u_i. \]
Require:

ixi=C.
A feasible allocation exists iff:
\[ \boxed{ \sum_i\ell_i \le C \le \sum_i u_i. } \]
Necessity
If:
\[ \ell_i\le x_i\le u_i \]
for all i, summing gives:
\[ \sum_i\ell_i \le \sum_i x_i = C \le \sum_i u_i. \]
Sufficiency
Set initially:
\[ x_i=\ell_i. \]
The remaining resource is:
\[ R=C-\sum_i\ell_i\ge0. \]
The total residual capacity is:
\[ \sum_i(u_i-\ell_i) = \sum_i u_i-\sum_i\ell_i \ge R. \]
Process stakeholders sequentially. At stakeholder i, add:
\[ y_i = \min \left\{ R_{\mathrm{current}}, u_i-\ell_i \right\} \]
and update:
\[ x_i=\ell_i+y_i, \qquad R_{\mathrm{next}}=R_{\mathrm{current}}-y_i. \]
Because aggregate residual capacity is at least the original R, this process reaches:

Rfinal=0.
The resulting allocation satisfies:
\[ \ell_i\le x_i\le u_i \]
and:

ixi=C.
∎
Consequence
If:
\[ \sum_i\ell_i>C, \]
the service floors are jointly physically infeasible. No fairness narrative can allocate more resource than exists.
Equal resource versus equal service
Equal allocations:

xi=xj
need not produce equal service if stakeholders possess different service-conversion maps:

si=hi(xi),sj=hj(xj),
with:
\[ h_i\neq h_j. \]
For example:

hi(x)=x,hj(x)=2x.
At:

xi=xj=1,
services are:

1,2.
Thus equal resource does not imply equal service.

13. Weighted Max-Min Allocation
DEF-SOC16 — Weighted Max-Min Objective
For weights:

wi>0,
define normalized service:

ri(x)=xiwi.
The weighted max-min objective is:
\[ \boxed{ \max_x \min_i \frac{x_i}{w_i}. } \]
THM-SOC9 — Weighted Max-Min Allocation on a Simplex Is Proportional to the Declared Weights
Statement
Let:
\[ \mathcal X_C = \left\{ x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^n: \sum_i x_i\le C \right\}, \qquad C>0. \]
Then the unique weighted max-min optimizer is:
\[ \boxed{ x_i^\star = \frac{Cw_i}{\sum_jw_j}. } \]
Proof
For any feasible x, define:

m(x)=ixiwi.
Then:
\[ x_i\ge m(x)w_i \]
for every i.
Summing:
\[ C \ge \sum_i x_i \ge m(x)\sum_iw_i. \]
Therefore:
\[ m(x) \le \frac{C}{\sum_iw_i}. \]
Now define:

xi=Cwijwj.
Then:

ixi=C,
and:

xiwi=Cjwj
for every i.
Thus x attains the upper bound.
For uniqueness, any optimizer attaining this bound must satisfy:
\[ x_i\ge \frac{Cw_i}{\sum_jw_j} \]
for every i. These lower bounds already sum to C. Since the allocation may not exceed C, equality must hold coordinatewise.
∎
Normative boundary
The theorem determines the weighted max-min solution given the weights. It does not establish that the weights are ethically, legally, or politically correct.



14. Weighted Proportional Fairness
DEF-SOC17 — Weighted Proportional Fairness
Let:
\[ \mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R_{>0}^n. \]
For weights:

wi>0,
allocation \(x^\star\in\mathcal X\) is weighted proportionally fair when:
\[ \boxed{ \sum_i w_i \frac{x_i-x_i^\star}{x_i^\star} \le0 \qquad \forall x\in\mathcal X. } \]
THM-SOC10 — Weighted Proportional Fairness Is Equivalent to Weighted Log-Utility Optimality on a Convex Positive Feasible Set
Statement
Assume:
\(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R_{>0}^n\) is nonempty and convex;
wi>0.
Define:

L(x)=iwixi.
Then \(x^\star\in\mathcal X\) maximizes L iff:
\[ \sum_i w_i \frac{x_i-x_i^\star}{x_i^\star} \le0 \qquad \forall x\in\mathcal X. \]
Forward direction
Take arbitrary \(x\in\mathcal X\). Define:
\[ h(t) = L\left( x^\star+t(x-x^\star) \right), \qquad 0\le t\le1. \]
Convexity of \(\mathcal X\) keeps the segment feasible.
Because x maximizes L, t=0 maximizes h over this interval, so:
\[ h'(0^+)\le0. \]
Now:

h'(0+)=L(x)(x-x).
Since:

Lxi(x)=wixi,
we obtain:
\[ h'(0^+) = \sum_i w_i \frac{x_i-x_i^\star}{x_i^\star} \le0. \]
Thus x is proportionally fair.
Reverse direction
Concavity of L gives:
\[ L(x) \le L(x^\star) + \nabla L(x^\star)\cdot(x-x^\star). \]
The assumed proportional-fairness inequality implies:
\[ \nabla L(x^\star)\cdot(x-x^\star)\le0. \]
Therefore:
\[ L(x)\le L(x^\star) \]
for every \(x\in\mathcal X\).
Thus x maximizes L.
∎
Scope
This equivalence depends on:
positivity;
convexity;
the exact weights;
the declared feasible set.
It is not a universal fairness theorem.

Proof

The associated marginal allocation m is budget balanced by the telescoping proof of THM-SOC16.
Now consider an arbitrary coalition SN.
Order the members of S as they appear in .
For iS, let:
Si: members of S preceding i;
Pi: all stakeholders preceding i in .
Then:

SiPi.
Submodularity gives diminishing marginal cost:
\[ C(P_i^\pi\cup\{i\})-C(P_i^\pi) \le C(S_i\cup\{i\})-C(S_i). \]

\[ m_i^\pi \le C(S_i\cup\{i\})-C(S_i). \]

\[ \sum_{i\in S} \left[ C(S_i\cup\{i\})-C(S_i) \right] = C(S)-C(\varnothing) = C(S). \]

49. Conjecture Registry
CONJ-INT1 — Sparse Cross-Layer Coupling
Most lower-layer packages interact through a small shared-object set.
Falsification: almost every internal variable becomes globally cross-layer relevant.
CONJ-INT2 — Global Witness Gluing Is Usually Locally Structured
Useful projects admit sparse compatibility structures sufficiently close to tree decompositions for practical gluing.
Falsification: ordinary projects exhibit dense inseparable global compatibility.
CONJ-INT3 — Assumption Debt Is Concentrated
A moderate number of unresolved assumptions usually controls final release.
Falsification: final assurance depends on thousands of equally critical unresolved assumptions.
CONJ-INT4 — Modal Errors Are Mechanically Detectable
Most accidental overclaims can be caught by explicit modality typing.
Falsification: important semantic strengthening routinely escapes the modality registry.
CONJ-INT5 — Theory Changes Usually Have Sparse Dependency Cones
Most theory changes reopen only a bounded proof slice.
Falsification: ordinary changes repeatedly force complete recertification.
CONJ-INT6 — Cyclic Assurance Components Are Small
Most assurance cycles can be encapsulated in moderate checked fixed-point or reachability nodes.
Falsification: one giant inseparable cycle dominates the project.
CONJ-INT7 — Trusted Kernel Can Remain Small
A comparatively small kernel can validate artifacts generated by highly sophisticated untrusted synthesis systems.
Falsification: sound checking requires trusting most solver internals.
CONJ-INT8 — Proof-DAG Sharing Is Material
Shared subproofs substantially reduce proof-storage and checking duplication.
Falsification: nearly every proof node remains semantically unique.
CONJ-INT9 — Incremental Final Recertification Usually Dominates Cold Checking
Routine changes can be recertified much faster than full reconstruction.
Falsification: dependency cones repeatedly approach the entire program.
CONJ-INT10 — Practical End-to-End Hotel PCFAR
The synthetic 190-room hotel admits a practical complete PCFAR.
Falsification: global compatibility, assumption closure, or proof-DAG complexity becomes prohibitive.
